sentences: There is nothing else to look at: a single black square inside a white border is all there is.
Yet this is one of the most famous paintings of the twentieth century, a square canvas 79.
5 centimetres on each side.
With this work the Russian avant-garde artist Kazimir Malevich launched Suprematism in 1915.
He called it the zero point of painting, a declaration that art would wipe the slate clean and start again from nothing.
The black square first appeared in 1913, in the stage designs Malevich created for the Futurist opera Victory over the Sun.
In the scene where the sun is defeated and dies, black squares filled the stage.
At the Last Futurist Exhibition 0,10 in Petrograd in 1915, he hung it high in the corner of the room.
That is the place a Russian home reserves for its icon, so Orthodox tradition and the new art met head-on.
Now look at the white border framing the black.
The edges are not perfectly ruler-straight; they waver slightly as they run along.
They reveal that this geometric square was painted by a human hand.
The black paint is thick, laid on in broad strokes whose marks remain.
From a distance it reads as a flat, even black, but up close the surface is uneven and full of texture, alive with the movement of the brush.
Now the web of cracks across the upper part.
Through the narrow gaps, faint traces of lighter colour glimmer from the layers beneath.
These cracks are partly the result of long neglect, and they show plainly the years this painting has lived through.
Under Stalin his work was banned, and the painting was hidden away in storage and neglected for decades.
It was not exhibited again until the 1980s.
The cracks speak of that long, enforced silence.
In 2015, X-rays revealed two earlier compositions hidden beneath the black paint: a brightly coloured Cubo-Futurist work and, painted over it, an early Suprematist design.
A handwritten inscription was found as well.
Malevich described such paintings as a desperate struggle to free art from the ballast of the objective world.
In later years he painted the same image three more times, and one of them, from 1929, is also in the Tretyakov Gallery.
Step back and look into the black for a while.
A square that at first seemed empty slowly begins to look different.
Standing before it, do you see an ending, or a beginning?
